title: Let the day perish (Job 3)
hook: Job curses the day he was born, and the Bible keeps his words

segments.voice: Yesterday, three friends on the ground with Job for seven days, saying nothing. Your line was they sat with him. Did you let someone lead, and stay quiet a moment longer? Day four hundred forty-four.

People say it when someone puts up with a lot: she has the patience of Job. The phrase comes from the letter of James in the New Testament, and it paints a picture of a man who suffers quietly, never raising his voice. Hold on to that picture for a moment. Because after seven days of silence on the ground, Job finally speaks. And the first thing out of his mouth, the opening of the long poem at the heart of the book, is not patient. It is not quiet. It is a curse.
screen: `THE PATIENCE OF JOB.` → `SEVEN DAYS OF SILENCE END.` → `NOT WHAT ANYONE EXPECTS.`

segments.voice: Chapter three begins, in the King James Bible: "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." Not God. His day. The day he was born. "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived." He wants that day erased from the calendar, the stars of that night to stay dark, the dawn never to come. Then the questions: "Why died I not from the womb?" Why is light given to someone in misery? And near the end: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me." Here's the striking thing about the book's shape. Chapters one and two are prose, like a story. Right here, with this curse, the book switches to poetry, and it stays poetry until the last page. The pain gets the poetry. And the Bible keeps every word. It doesn't cut this chapter or soften it. The prophet Jeremiah says something close, in his own book: cursed be the day wherein I was born. Two people of faith, saying the unsayable, and scripture keeps both. Now back to James. The Greek word translated patience there is hupomone, which the lexicons give as endurance or steadfastness: holding on under a weight without walking away. That fits Job better than quiet ever did. Job never stops talking to God, even when he's shouting. He doesn't leave. Christians have often called this kind of speech lament, prayer that tells God the truth about how bad it is. On this reading, even a curse on your birthday, said to God, is still a way of staying in the conversation.
screen: `HE CURSES HIS DAY, NOT GOD` · `FROM PROSE INTO POETRY` · `THE BIBLE KEEPS EVERY WORD` · `PATIENCE MEANS ENDURANCE` · then, large: `LET THE DAY PERISH WHEREIN I WAS BORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your honest lament. Take a piece of paper, or your phone's notes. Write what is actually hard right now, in plain words. Don't tidy it. Don't add a lesson at the end. If you're angry, write angry. If you're tired of something, say so. A few lines is plenty. Then stop, and sit with what you wrote for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can offer it to God as it is, unpolished, the way Job did. If you don't, let it simply be true on the page. The bell holds the time.
Hupomone. Greek for endurance, steadfastness that holds on without walking away, the word James really means by Job's patience, even as Job curses the day he was born.

Your line: even this is prayer. Today, if something hard comes up, don't polish it. Say it honestly, once, to God if you pray or to yourself if you don't, and let that count. Day four hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray laments, honest complaints brought to God, using the words of Job, the psalms of lament and Lamentations, and some churches hold services of lament after tragedies.

original.note: Hebrew: let the day perish. the first words of Job's curse in 3:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: Job is the patient man who never complained.
what it means: after a week of silence he curses his birthday, and scripture keeps it, as honest speech to God.
what a scholar hears: the book turns from prose to poetry here, and James 5:11's 'patience' is hupomone, endurance.

notes: Editor pass (y2 review): cut the superlative 'one of the darkest speeches anywhere in the Bible', 'the line many sufferers have recognized', and the count 'almost forty chapters' (now 'until the last page'); hupomone glossed from the lexicon rather than as a word origin; carry no longer assumes the listener speaks to God.
James 5:11 KJV 'Ye have heard of the patience of Job'; Greek hupomone = endurance, steadfastness. Paraphrased in voice. Confirm.
Prose/poetry structure: prose 1:1–2:13 and 42:7–17; poetry 3:1–42:6. 'Almost forty chapters' = chapters 3 through 42:6. Confirm.
